- Past incrementalism doesn't guarantee future pace. If reasoning and test-time compute dominate the next phase, that looks more like a paradigm shift.

## From the chat

- The chat called ~3×/year "pure algorithmic efficiency, hardware and competition stripped out," the most conservative rung in its "honest hierarchy" of cost-decline numbers.
- It cited Epoch: pre-training compute efficiency improving "roughly 3.0× per year," letting capability grow without matching growth in parameters.
- On breakthroughs versus tweaks: "A breakthrough like MoE or the Transformer doesn't itself deliver the cost drop; it resets the ceiling, and then years of engineering grind the cost down toward the new ceiling."
- It flagged that this synthesis was its own reasoning and that future drivers are genuinely uncertain.

rates.overview: This hub gathers every growth or decline rate quoted in the chat, with its method and source, so they can be compared on one footing. Most are expressed as a **factor per year**. Some are measured from disclosed data: [Epoch](#c/epoch)'s 3.4×/year growth in AI chip stock, 5×/year growth in frontier training compute, and ~3×/year pre-training efficiency. Some are controlled estimates, such as the [price-trend paper](#c/price-paper)'s 5–10× and ~3× inference-price declines and the [open-model](#c/open-price) 7–28×. Some are forecasts or framings, such as McKinsey's GW projection, JLL's 14% CAGR and Nvidia's 1,000,000×. [Moore's law](#c/e-moore) is included only for scale. The chat's key lesson is that the rates are more trustworthy than dollar forecasts, and that the method, especially frozen list prices, can move a "rate" by two orders of magnitude. See [Cost at a fixed capability](#c/fixed-capability).

quantization.overview: Weight quantization stores and computes a model's weights at lower numerical precision, for example **FP8, INT8 or INT4** instead of 16-bit. Because [inference is memory-bound](#c/memory-bound), fewer bytes per weight means less data to move per token, a smaller memory footprint and more concurrent requests per GPU, all of which lower [cost per token](#c/cost-per-token). The chat lists it among the core [serving optimizations](#c/serving-opts) that make a frozen model cheaper, "often with negligible quality loss," though some accuracy loss is possible. Related forms appear elsewhere in the graph. [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3) trains natively in FP8 and ships only FP8 weights (`quant_method: "fp8"`). [KV-cache quantization](#c/kv-quant) applies the idea to cached keys and values. [QLoRA](#c/qlora) quantizes a frozen base to 4-bit for cheap fine-tuning.
quantization.article:
**Weight quantization** means representing a neural network's weights, and often its activations, with fewer bits than the 16-bit floating point (FP16 or BF16) they are usually trained in. Common targets are **8-bit** (FP8 or INT8) and **4-bit** (INT4). It is one of the standard [serving optimizations](#c/serving-opts) that make an already-trained model cheaper to run, and it modifies the model's [numeric precision](#c/weights-precision).

## How it works

Each weight is mapped from a high-precision value to a lower-precision one using a scale factor, and sometimes an offset, chosen per tensor, per channel or per small group of weights. At inference the low-precision values are either computed on directly by hardware that supports the format, or expanded back ("dequantized") just before use. The main variants are:

- **Post-training quantization.** Quantize a finished model, often using a small calibration dataset to pick scales that minimize error. It needs no retraining, which is why it counts as a frozen-weights optimization.
- **Quantization-aware training.** Simulate low precision during training so the model learns to tolerate it.
- **Native low-precision training.** Train in the low-precision format from the start. [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3) trains natively in FP8 and publishes only FP8 weights, with a script to convert to BF16.

## Why it cuts cost

Because [inference is memory-bound](#c/memory-bound), the cost of generating a token is dominated by moving weights and cache out of HBM. Halving the bytes per weight (16-bit to 8-bit) roughly halves that traffic for the weights. Going to 4-bit quarters it. The effects compound:

| Effect | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Fewer bytes read per token | Faster generation on the same chip |
| Smaller model footprint | Fits on fewer GPUs; less cross-chip communication |
| Freed HBM | More room for [KV-caches](#c/kv-cache), so more concurrent requests |
| Native low-precision math on newer chips | Higher arithmetic throughput too |

All of these lower [serving cost per token](#c/cost-per-token), which makes quantization a key reason a *frozen* model gets cheaper over its life.

## Related forms

- **[KV-cache quantization](#c/kv-quant)**: storing cached keys and values in 8-bit or lower. The chat notes keys tend to be more sensitive than values, so schemes sometimes quantize them differently.
- **[QLoRA](#c/qlora)**: quantizes a frozen base model to 4-bit while training small [LoRA](#c/lora) adapters at higher precision, which brings fine-tuning of large models onto consumer hardware.

## Trade-offs

Lower precision discards information. At 8-bit the quality loss is often negligible for large models. At 4-bit and below, results depend more on the method, the model and the task, and outlier weights or activations need special handling. The chat's phrasing, "often with negligible quality loss," reflects this: often, not always. There is also a hardware dependence. The speed-up is largest when the chip natively supports the format, and a well-established trend is that newer [hardware generations](#c/hardware-gens) add support for ever-lower precisions.

## From the chat

The chat covers quantization only briefly, so this article relies on general, well-established knowledge for the mechanics.

- It listed quantization, "running the model at lower numerical precision, FP8/INT8/INT4, often with negligible quality loss," among the serving optimizations that make a frozen Sonnet-like model cheaper.
- It classed KV-cache quantization as a pure serving trick that works on frozen weights, noting the quality-vs-size trade-off and that keys are more sensitive than values.
- It pointed out that DeepSeek-V3's config shows `quant_method: "fp8"`: FP8 training is native to its framework, so only FP8 weights are provided.
- It described QLoRA as quantizing the frozen base to 4-bit while keeping adapters at higher precision.

spec-decoding.overview: Speculative decoding speeds up generation without changing the output. A small, fast **draft model** proposes several next tokens, and the large model **verifies them in one parallel pass**, accepting the longest correct prefix and resampling where they diverge. Large-model decoding is [memory-bound](#c/memory-bound), and checking several tokens costs about as much as generating one, so every accepted guess is nearly free throughput. With the standard acceptance rule, the output distribution matches the big model exactly. The chat lists it among the core [serving optimizations](#c/serving-opts) that lower a frozen model's [cost per token](#c/cost-per-token). It also notes that DeepSeek-V3's [Multi-Token Prediction](#c/mtp) heads, trained to predict several future tokens, "double as a speculative-decoding accelerator at inference." It modifies the ordinary [decoding loop](#c/decoding).
spec-decoding.article:
**Speculative decoding** is an inference technique that generates text from a large language model faster by letting a cheap *draft* process guess upcoming tokens and having the large *target* model check those guesses in parallel. With the standard acceptance rule, the output is statistically identical to what the target model would have produced alone. That makes it a pure [serving optimization](#c/serving-opts) that works on frozen weights.

## The problem it solves

Ordinary autoregressive generation, the [decoding loop](#c/decoding), produces one token per forward pass of the full model, and each pass has to stream the model's weights from memory. Because [inference is memory-bound](#c/memory-bound), a pass that checks five tokens costs about the same wall-clock time as a pass that produces one. The large model spends most of each step waiting on memory, not doing arithmetic. Speculative decoding puts that idle arithmetic to work.

## How it works

1. **Draft.** A small, fast model (or cheap extra prediction heads on the big model) proposes the next *k* tokens one after another. Each draft step is cheap.
2. **Verify.** The large model runs **one** forward pass over the context plus all *k* drafted tokens, producing its own probabilities at each position in parallel.
3. **Accept or reject.** Moving left to right, each draft token is accepted with a probability based on how the target's probabilities compare with the draft's. At the first rejection, a corrected token is sampled from an adjusted distribution and the rest of the draft is discarded.
4. **Repeat** from the new position.

Every step yields at least one token and at best *k*+1, so the speed-up depends on the **acceptance rate**, which is how often the draft agrees with the target. Predictable text, such as code, boilerplate or common phrasing, gets high acceptance.

## Variants

- **Separate draft model**: a smaller model from the same family, sharing the tokenizer.
- **Self-speculation with extra heads**: the model is trained with additional heads that predict tokens further ahead. The chat notes that DeepSeek-V3's [Multi-Token Prediction](#c/mtp) objective, which predicts several future tokens while keeping a causal chain, is primarily a training signal, and that its extra heads "double as a speculative-decoding accelerator at inference."

## Trade-offs

| Benefit | Cost |
|---|---|
| Lower latency per token | Must run and host a draft model (or train extra heads) |
| More tokens per pass over the weights | Wasted verification work when guesses are rejected |
| Exact output distribution (standard scheme) | Gains shrink when text is unpredictable or batches are already large |

The interaction with batching matters. In a heavily batched server the large model is already busier, so the idle compute that speculative decoding exploits is smaller. How much it saves depends on the workload and the serving setup.

## Relation to cost

Faster generation per request frees accelerator time for other requests, which lowers [serving cost per token](#c/cost-per-token) for the same frozen model. It is one of the techniques behind the chat's answer that a given model does get cheaper to run over its life, through serving work, in lumps. Diffusion language models pursue a related goal, generating several tokens in parallel, through a different architecture ([Diffusion language models](#c/diffusion-lm)).

## From the chat

The chat treated speculative decoding in only a sentence or two. The mechanics above are standard, well-established material, not from the chat.

- It described it as "a small draft model proposes tokens a big model verifies in parallel," listed among the serving optimizations that make a frozen model cheaper.
- It noted that DeepSeek-V3's MTP heads double as a speculative-decoding accelerator at inference.
- It gave no numbers on speed-ups or on which providers use it.

cont-batching.overview: Continuous batching, also called dynamic or in-flight batching, is a scheduling technique for LLM servers. Instead of waiting for a whole batch of requests to finish before starting the next, the server **swaps requests in and out at every generation step**: finished sequences leave, and queued ones take their slots. Requests produce very different numbers of tokens, so static [batching](#c/batching) leaves the accelerator partly idle while it waits for the longest one. Continuous batching keeps it saturated. Because [inference is memory-bound](#c/memory-bound), each pass over the weights can serve many requests, so higher occupancy directly lowers [cost per token](#c/cost-per-token). The chat lists it among the core [serving optimizations](#c/serving-opts) that work on frozen weights and pair naturally with [PagedAttention](#c/paged-attn), which frees memory for more concurrent requests.
cont-batching.article:
**Continuous batching** (also called *dynamic*, *iteration-level* or *in-flight* batching) is a way of scheduling requests on an LLM inference server so that the batch being processed changes at every token-generation step instead of staying fixed until every request in it finishes. It is one of the most important [serving optimizations](#c/serving-opts) for throughput, and it works on any frozen model. It modifies plain [batching](#c/batching).

## The problem with static batching

Batching is essential for inference economics. Because [inference is memory-bound](#c/memory-bound), one read of the model's weights from HBM can serve many requests at once, so throughput grows with batch size at little extra cost.

With **static batching**, the server gathers a group of requests, runs them together until *all* are done, then starts the next group. LLM requests vary enormously in length. One might need 20 output tokens and another 2,000. Under static batching:

- finished requests leave empty slots that sit idle until the longest request finishes,
- new requests wait in the queue even though capacity is free, which hurts latency,
- the GPU's effective utilization can be low.

## How continuous batching works

The scheduler works at the level of **individual decoding iterations**:

1. At each step, the model generates one token for every active sequence in the batch.
2. Any sequence that has finished (end-of-sequence token or length limit) is removed right away.
3. Waiting requests are admitted into the freed slots, with their prompts processed, then join the ongoing generation.
4. Repeat.

The batch becomes a rolling pool, so the accelerator stays saturated as long as there is demand. The idea was popularized in LLM-serving research and systems around 2022–2023 (the Orca scheduler and then vLLM, among others) and is now standard in production serving stacks.

## Why it needs memory management

Admitting a new request mid-flight requires room for its [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache), which grows with every generated token. Reserving a maximum-length contiguous block for each request wastes memory and caps how many can be admitted. That is why continuous batching pairs naturally with [PagedAttention](#c/paged-attn), which stores the cache in small pages allocated on demand, and with cache-shrinking techniques like [KV quantization](#c/kv-quant) and [GQA](#c/gqa). More free memory means more concurrent sequences, which means more tokens per pass over the weights.

## Effects on cost and latency

| Metric | Effect |
|---|---|
| Throughput (tokens/GPU-second) | Rises substantially: fewer idle slots |
| [Cost per token](#c/cost-per-token) | Falls, since the same hardware serves more tokens |
| Queueing latency | Falls: requests start without waiting for a batch to drain |
| Per-token latency | Can rise slightly under heavy load as batches grow |

Providers tune the trade-off between batch size (cheaper per token) and latency (faster per user). Mixing long prompt-processing steps with ongoing generation adds further scheduling complexity, and serving systems use various techniques to balance the two.

## From the chat

The chat mentions continuous batching only in passing. The mechanics and history above are standard, well-established material, not from the chat.

- It named "better batching (continuous/dynamic batching to keep accelerators saturated)" first among the serving optimizations that make a frozen model like a given Sonnet cheaper to run.
- In describing a modern serving stack (GQA model, FlashAttention, PagedAttention, prefix caching, KV quantization), it listed "continuous batching to keep the accelerator saturated" as part of the standard combination.
- It gave no throughput figures and said it couldn't confirm what any specific proprietary provider runs.

epoch.overview: Epoch AI is an independent research organization that tracks AI trends such as compute, model size, training runs and inference prices, using public disclosures, revenue data and published prices. The chat relied on it more than any other source and called it one of "the most neutral". It is not selling chips, real estate or models. Its figures in the chat: AI chip compute stock growing **3.4×/year** ([e-stock](#c/e-stock)), frontier training compute **5×/year** ([e-train](#c/e-train)), pre-training efficiency **~3×/year** ([e-pretrain-eff](#c/e-pretrain-eff)), inference price at fixed capability falling **9–900×/year** ([e-price-all](#c/e-price-all)), and the parameter-count history, including the post-GPT-4 shrink. Its limits, which it flags itself: price trends built from current list prices are inflated by frozen proprietary prices, the fastest rates are recent and may not last, and closed-model parameter counts are estimates. See [the ~100×/year claim](#c/c-100x).

price-paper.overview: The inference price-trend paper (arXiv **2511.23455**) is an academic study of how fast the price of reaching a given benchmark score falls, designed to control for the confounds in headline figures. The chat drew on it (partly through an alphaXiv summary) for three results. First, frontier price-for-performance falls about **5–10× per year** once frozen list prices are accounted for ([e-price-frontier](#c/e-price-frontier)). Second, isolating algorithmic efficiency, by dividing out hardware price declines and controlling for competition using open models, gives **~3× per year** ([e-price-algo](#c/e-price-algo)). Third, declines are fastest at high capability: **31×/year** in the top GPQA-Diamond bin against **1.7×/year** in the bottom ([e-price-top](#c/e-price-top)). The authors suggest distillation or MoE may explain the gap. It therefore both [challenges the ~100×/year headline](#c/c-100x) and [supports faster declines at the frontier](#c/c-frontier-fastest).

open-price.overview: This is a LessWrong analysis of how fast algorithmic progress lowers inference prices. Its key methodological move is to use **open-weight models**. Proprietary developers "tend not to change the inference price of older models," so their frozen list prices sit next to cheap new models and inflate apparent declines. Open weights are served by many competing hosts, which avoids those list-price games. The analysis finds open-model prices at fixed capability falling a fairly steady **7–28× per year, geometric mean ~11.8×** ([e-price-open](#c/e-price-open)), and fairly **uniform across quality levels**. It therefore [challenges the ~100×/year headline](#c/c-100x) and complicates the claim that [declines are fastest at the frontier](#c/c-frontier-fastest). The same piece also notes that across studies prices dropped more for top models. It is a blog-hosted analysis, not peer-reviewed; the chat treats it as a clean independent read.

nvidia.overview: Nvidia, and its CEO Jensen Huang, is the dominant seller of AI accelerators, taking the overwhelming majority of accelerator spend. That makes it both an essential source and an **interested party**. The chat drew several things from Nvidia. There were its audited results: record fiscal Q3 2026 data-center revenue of $51.2B, with [Blackwell sold out](#c/blackwell). There was its GTC framing that computing demand grew ~**1,000,000× in two years** ([e-demand](#c/e-demand)), made up of ~10,000× per request and ~100× usage. And there were Huang's escalating forecasts, from $500B of high-confidence demand through 2026 to at least **$1 trillion through 2027**, along with "we are going to be short." The chat called the trillion-dollar figures "the most interest-conflicted" in the discussion, noting that Nvidia sells the chips, while accepting that the direction is corroborated elsewhere. It [supports](#c/c-squeeze) the view that frontier scarcity lasts into 2027–28.

semianalysis.overview: SemiAnalysis is a semiconductor and AI-infrastructure research firm whose estimates get re-reported widely. In the chat it is the source for the claim that **memory could be ~30% of hyperscaler AI spending in 2026, up from ~8% in 2023–24** ([e-hbm](#c/e-hbm)), and, in the chat's words, for "a SemiAnalysis-type read" that chip production became "a binding constraint on the pace of the AI compute buildout" in late 2025 and early 2026. This graph also attributes the **+36% 2026 capex** figure to it ([e-capex](#c/e-capex)). The chat itself quoted that figure from secondary coverage based on company guidance. The chat classes SemiAnalysis with McKinsey and Bloomberg Intelligence as the few analyst shops behind many widely echoed numbers. Its percentages are therefore "directional analyst estimates, not hard facts," and repeated citations shouldn't be counted as independent confirmation. See [HBM supply](#c/hbm-supply).

mckinsey.overview: McKinsey is a management consultancy whose data-center projections the chat called "the one to anchor on" for the longer horizon. Its figure is that global data-center supply could grow from about **70 GW today to about 220 GW within five years**, with around **75% of the growth driven by AI** ([Data centers: ~70 → ~220 GW](#c/dc-growth), [e-dc](#c/e-dc)). That is roughly a tripling, or about 26% a year compounded. It is a capacity forecast, not a measurement, and it doesn't account explicitly for the [slips](#c/slip) already pushing 2026 projects into 2028. The chat groups McKinsey with SemiAnalysis and Bloomberg Intelligence as analyst shops whose numbers get echoed across many outlets. It is less interested than a chipmaker, but its percentages are still best read as directional. [JLL](#c/jll)'s ~14% CAGR is a more conservative comparison point.

jll.overview: JLL is a commercial real-estate firm whose data-center outlook supplied the chat's view of the long-run workload mix. By its estimates, AI was about a quarter of data-center workloads in 2025, mostly training. [Inference overtakes training in 2027](#c/inference-shift), and AI could be half of all workloads by 2030. It also expects nearly 100 GW of new capacity between 2026 and 2030, the sector growing at a **~14% CAGR** ([e-dc-jll](#c/e-dc-jll)), and a buildout needing up to $3 trillion by 2030. The chat classes JLL as having a position, since real-estate analysts benefit from the buildout. JLL does name a real fragility in its own bull case: the inference supercycle depends on inference applications that "don't yet exist at scale." Its growth rate is noticeably lower than [McKinsey](#c/mckinsey)'s.

accuris.overview: Accuris (an electronics-component supply-chain analysis firm) and Tech Insider (a trade publication) are the chat's main sources on the physical side of the [capacity constraint](#c/capacity). Accuris reported that **30–50% of planned 2026 AI data-center capacity is projected to slip to 2028** because of interconnection queues and construction bottlenecks ([slip](#c/slip)). It also reported that HBM now uses ~23% of DRAM wafer capacity, and that the spending is "funded, contracted, and under construction." Tech Insider reported transformer lead times stretching from 12–18 to **36–48 months**, gave a starker estimate that ~50% of planned US 2026 data centers could be delayed or cancelled, and placed the shift to electrical gear as the bottleneck around May 2026. These are analyst and trade sources, and they [support](#c/c-squeeze) the view that frontier scarcity lasts into 2027–28. The chat found them useful because they describe hard physical lead times, not demand projections.

stanford-toy.overview: The Stanford teaching model is a course page (Stanford MSE 435) that sets out supply-and-demand scenarios for AI compute. It **explicitly calls itself a pedagogical toy, not a forecast**, and the chat cited it only "for the framework, not predictions." Its scenarios: through 2025–26, TSMC expands capacity while data-center power struggles to keep up. If demand growth slows to ~100% a year, supply might catch up and the gap close (the "AI winter" case, where investment returns get harder). An energy breakthrough would move the bottleneck to memory bandwidth. If everything improves equally, no single chokepoint remains and margins compress across the stack. Because it sketches a way supply could catch up, it serves as a [counterpoint](#c/c-squeeze) to the view that scarcity lasts until 2027–28. It is academic and has no commercial stake. See [capacity constraint](#c/capacity).

rlvr-study.overview: This is an academic study that tested reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards ([RLVR](#c/rlvr)) across algorithms including PPO and [GRPO](#c/grpo). Its deflating finding: RLVR **increases the likelihood of correct samples but decreases coverage of solvable problems**. It makes a model better at producing high-reward answers it could already produce, but doesn't give it abilities beyond the base model's reach. It contrasts this with [distillation](#c/distillation), which can transfer genuinely new reasoning patterns from a stronger teacher, and it notes that current RLVR algorithms perform similarly to one another and remain far from optimal. It [challenges](#c/c-rlvr-new) the claim that RLVR creates new reasoning ability. The chat later cautioned that it is one paper's framing, and that it doesn't measure how much of any model's reasoning came from distillation.

tulu3.overview: Tülu 3, from the Allen Institute for AI (Ai2), is the rare project that open-sourced an *entire* post-training recipe: model weights, datasets, a data-curation and evaluation toolkit, training code and a reproduction guide. Its 405B version competes with GPT-4o-mini, Claude 3.5 Haiku and DeepSeek-V3, so the chat treats it as a frontier-relevant view into what closed labs do. Its most cited disclosure is that all of its new **synthetic SFT datasets contain responses written by GPT-4o or Claude 3.5 Sonnet** (the latter for coding), because those gave the best responses. That makes it direct evidence that [distillation from closed models](#c/c-distill-open) is part of open post-training, at least for SFT data. It is an independent, fully transparent source. See [synthetic SFT responses](#c/synthetic-sft) and [post-training](#c/post-training).

dclm.overview: DCLM (DataComp for Language Models) is a benchmark in which the model architecture and training setup are **held fixed and only the data-curation strategy varies**. It turns data selection into a competition over which curation method gives the best model for the same compute. The chat argued that the benchmark's very existence shows where the field's attention has moved: "You don't build a whole competitive testbed around a variable unless it's where the action is." Its headline result is that **DCLM-Baseline beat the prior open-data state of the art by ~6 MMLU points while using half the compute**, which [supports](#c/c-data-lever) the claim that data curation is the biggest lever. DCLM-Baseline also illustrates heavy [deduplication](#c/dedup) and [model-based quality filtering](#c/quality-filter). It is an academic source, and its evidence is controlled by design.

vl-study.overview: This is a vision-language instruction-tuning study the chat cited as direct evidence that specialists can beat a generalist on their own tasks. The researchers split the training data by task and compared one model tuned on everything against task experts tuned only on their relevant subsets. **On 5 of 7 downstream tasks, the all-data model was outperformed by the task expert.** The chat paired it with an expert-LM paper that explains the mechanism, negative task transfer, and reports a +10.4% mean accuracy gain from selecting relevant experts at inference. It [supports](#c/c-specialists) the specialist claim. The chat's caveats: this evidence comes mostly from SFT and smaller-scale or vision-language settings, very large models seem to absorb diverse tasks with less interference, and one careful study is not established law. See [Specialize, then merge](#c/merging).

robustness-paper.overview: This is a 2026 security paper finding that Mamba–Transformer [hybrids](#c/hybrids) inherit a new **robustness vulnerability** from their [Mamba](#c/mamba) components. Under certain hidden-state-poisoning triggers, even the 52B Jamba-1.7-Mini hybrid collapses on a robustness benchmark while pure Transformers do not, and the weakness extends to Mamba-2-based hybrids such as [Nemotron-H](#c/nemotron-h). It [challenges](#c/c-hybrid-parity) the claim that hybrids match transformers at large scale. Quality parity on capability benchmarks doesn't rule out trade-offs those benchmarks can't see. The chat asked readers to hold it loosely: "early research, one paper, on a specific attack class", something "to watch rather than a settled verdict." It is an academic source with no evident commercial stake.

no-free-lunch.overview: This is a May 2026 survey titled "A Comparative Survey of Inference Acceleration for DLLMs against AR-LLMs: No Free Lunch." It compares the speed-ups claimed for [diffusion language models](#c/diffusion-lm) against autoregressive models under careful conditions. The chat hadn't read it in depth, and said the title alone signals its thesis: the parallel-generation speed advantage isn't free, and the quality/speed/compute triangle has costs that headline tokens-per-second figures obscure. It therefore [challenges](#c/c-diffusion-parity) the claim that diffusion LMs match autoregressive quality at 5–10× the speed, most of whose support comes from vendors' own benchmarks. The chat called it "probably the most intellectually honest next stop" and "the corrective to all the vendor benchmarks." The paper postdated the chat's knowledge, so it was relaying the source, not confirming it.

vendor-claims.overview: Vendor announcements are benchmark results and capability claims published by a model's own developer, such as launch posts, technical reports and marketing. The chat treated them as **self-reported**: often real, but not independently verified. Examples in the chat include NVIDIA's framing that [Nemotron-H](#c/nemotron-h) hybrids are state-of-the-art with faster inference, Meta's results for BLT and LCM ("matches Llama 3", partly at 8B scale), and Gemini Diffusion's and Mercury's coding benchmarks. They [support](#c/c-hybrid-parity) the claim that hybrids match transformers at scale, but the chat wanted independent replication before accepting general parity. Its pattern for weighing them: note the scale tested, the domains covered (often just coding and math) and who ran the evaluation, and compare against independent critiques such as the [robustness paper](#c/robustness-paper).

glm52-early.overview: This is the first wave of reporting on Zhipu's (Z.ai's) [GLM-5.2](#c/glm-52), written **June 13–15, 2026** around its release. It was emphatic that Zhipu published **no official benchmark scores** at launch: no SWE-bench Verified, no LiveCodeBench, no HumanEval. One outlet called this unusual for a release of that scale and said the numbers "should be treated as marketing promises until independent verification arrives." It did confirm concrete additions: a one-million-token context (about 5× the GLM-5 line's 200K), High and Max reasoning-effort modes, and rollout across all GLM Coding Plan tiers with MIT-licensed open weights to follow. It [challenges](#c/c-glm52) the later claim that GLM-5.2 beats GPT-5.5 on long-horizon coding. It is analyst and press coverage, and the chat judged it the more careful wave.

glm52-late.overview: This is the second wave of [GLM-5.2](#c/glm-52) coverage, from **June 16–17, 2026**, which suddenly carried strong benchmark claims. It described GLM-5.2 as a 753-billion-parameter open-weights model that **beats GPT-5.5 on multiple long-horizon coding benchmarks at one-sixth the cost**. One outlet added that it scored above Claude Opus 4.7 and, in some human blind tests, outperformed Claude Fable 5. It [supports](#c/c-glm52) the GLM-5.2 coding claim, but the chat was skeptical. The claims appear only in the newest, partly aggregated coverage. They contradict the "no benchmarks at launch" reporting from two days earlier ([early coverage](#c/glm52-early)). They read like vendor launch framing. And the chat couldn't verify the comparison models. It treated the blind-test claim as "unverified marketing" pending independent evaluation.

e-stock.overview: This is [Epoch AI](#c/epoch)'s estimate that the total computing power of the installed stock of AI chips has grown about **3.4× per year since 2022**, doubling roughly every **7 months**. It is built from revenue data, financial disclosures and analyst reports, and measures what was actually delivered, not what was ordered or forecast. The chat anchored on it as the most methodologically careful demand-side number, noting that a 7-month doubling sustained over years is far faster than [Moore's law](#c/e-moore) (~2 years). It is a *supply delivered* figure that serves as a proxy for demand, so it understates demand when capacity is short. It doesn't show how compute is split between training and inference, or between providers. See [compute demand](#c/compute-demand) and [available compute](#c/compute-supply).

e-train.overview: This is [Epoch AI](#c/epoch)'s estimate that the training compute used for frontier language models has grown about **5× per year since 2020**, doubling roughly every **5.2 months**. It is measured from tracked training runs. The chat used it to show that "scale" and "parameter count" have come apart. Epoch attributes about two-thirds of the past decade's language-model gains to scale, meaning *training compute*, and that compute kept growing 5× a year even as frontier parameter counts [fell after GPT-4](#c/e-params-shrink). Labs spent the extra compute on more data and longer training of moderately sized models, following [Chinchilla](#c/chinchilla), not on ever-bigger models. The rate covers training only, and says nothing about inference demand or cost. See [pre-training](#c/pretraining).

e-demand.overview: This is [Nvidia](#c/nvidia)'s GTC framing that computing demand grew roughly **1,000,000× over two years**, about 1,000× per year. It is the product of two stylized multipliers: ~**10,000×** more compute per inference session as models moved from chatbots to [reasoning and agentic systems](#c/reasoning-load), and ~**100×** more [usage](#c/usage-growth). It is a keynote framing, not a measurement, and it comes from the company that sells the chips. The chat used it for its *qualitative* point: per-request compute is multiplying on top of user growth, which is why the demand curve is bending up. It doesn't match measured hardware growth ([3.4×/year](#c/e-stock)), because it describes what workloads would want, not what was installed. Read it as directional.

e-capex.overview: Major cloud companies are expected to spend **over $600 billion on capex in 2026, up 36% from 2025**, with about **$450 billion** going to AI infrastructure. The figure comes from company guidance reported in secondary coverage, and this graph attributes it to [SemiAnalysis](#c/semianalysis). Accuris described the spending as "funded, contracted, and under construction rather than speculative." The chat used it to make the point that spending on this scale still can't quickly buy past physical lead times. It measures money committed, not compute delivered, and a meaningful share will land later than planned because of [slips](#c/slip). As a single-year growth rate it is guidance, and can be revised. See [Hyperscaler capex](#c/capex).

e-dc.overview: [McKinsey](#c/mckinsey)'s projection that global data-center supply could grow from about **70 GW to about 220 GW within five years**, roughly a tripling, with ~75% of growth driven by AI. Annualized, that is about **1.26× per year** (~26% compounded). It is a capacity forecast measured in power, not compute, so it isn't directly comparable with Epoch's [3.4×/year](#c/e-stock) chip-compute growth. Each watt buys more compute as chips improve. It is also more optimistic than [JLL](#c/jll)'s ~14% CAGR ([e-dc-jll](#c/e-dc-jll)), and it doesn't account explicitly for the [delays](#c/slip) pushing 2026 projects to 2028. The chat called it "the one to anchor on" for the longer horizon. See [Data centers: ~70 → ~220 GW](#c/dc-growth).

e-dc-jll.overview: This is [JLL](#c/jll)'s sector outlook: data-center capacity growing at about **14% a year (CAGR) to 2030**, with nearly **100 GW** of new capacity expected online between 2026 and 2030 and a buildout requiring up to **$3 trillion** by 2030. The chat used it as the basis for timing supply relief, reading it as saying that physical supply loosens meaningfully around [2027–28](#c/capacity-relief), if demand growth also slows. It is noticeably lower than the ~26%/year implied by [McKinsey's projection](#c/e-dc). The difference reflects different scopes and assumptions, and neither is a measurement. JLL is a real-estate firm with a position in the buildout, so the chat treats its forecasts as coming from an interested party.

e-hbm.overview: This is [SemiAnalysis](#c/semianalysis)'s estimate that memory could account for about **30% of hyperscaler AI spending in 2026, up from about 8% in 2023 and 2024**. Taken over three years, the share grows roughly 1.55× a year. The chat used it to show that [HBM](#c/hbm-supply) has gone "from a rounding error to a major cost center," consistent with SK Hynix selling out for 2026 and HBM taking ~23% of DRAM wafer capacity. It also follows from [inference being memory-bound](#c/memory-bound): memory bandwidth and capacity drive serving throughput. It is an analyst spend estimate ("could account for"), re-reported widely, so the chat treats it as directional. It describes a share of spending, not a physical quantity.

e-price-all.overview: This is [Epoch AI](#c/epoch)'s finding that the price of reaching a fixed level of performance fell by anywhere from **9× to 900× per year**, depending on the capability bar, using **all models at their current list prices**. This is the source of the famous "~100× per year / halving every 2 months" summary ([the claim](#c/c-100x)). The chat stressed three caveats. First, there is no single rate, only a family of lines. Second, the fastest declines happened in the most recent year, and Epoch itself flags that they may not persist. Third, proprietary developers rarely cut the prices of old models, so frozen list prices inflate the apparent decline. Controlled estimates are far lower ([5–10×](#c/e-price-frontier), [~3×](#c/e-price-algo)). It measures [cost at a fixed capability](#c/fixed-capability), not the cost of any given model.

e-price-top.overview: This is the [price-trend paper](#c/price-paper)'s breakdown by capability. Models in the **highest GPQA-Diamond bin fell in price 31× per year**, while those in the **lowest bin fell only 1.7× per year**. This went against the user's hypothesis that [higher bars take cheap models longer to catch](#c/m-harder). The chat's explanation: high bars are *new*, so the first cheaper model to match an expensive frontier model is a large multiplier, while low bars were cleared years ago and have little cost left to remove. The authors suggest greater use of [distillation](#c/distillation) or MoE at the top. It [supports](#c/c-frontier-fastest) the view that declines are fastest at the frontier, but [open-model data](#c/e-price-open) shows a more uniform pattern, and the top-end rates are recent.

e-price-open.overview: The [open-model price analysis](#c/open-price) finds that among **open-weight models only**, the price of reaching a fixed capability fell **7–28× per year, with a geometric mean of about 11.8×**, and fairly uniformly across quality levels. Open weights give a cleaner read because many hosts compete to serve the same model, so there are no frozen proprietary list prices inflating the trend ([Price ≠ serving cost](#c/price-vs-cost)). The chat placed this range in the middle of its "honest hierarchy": below the confounded [9–900×](#c/e-price-all) headline and above the [~3×](#c/e-price-algo) algorithmic floor. Its uniformity across quality [cuts against](#c/c-frontier-fastest) the finding that declines are fastest at the frontier. It still measures prices, and only for open models, which may not track closed frontier ones.

e-price-frontier.overview: This is the [price-trend paper](#c/price-paper)'s estimate that, after controlling for frozen list prices, the price for a given benchmark performance level falls about **5–10× per year for frontier models**. The chat called the surrounding ~5–12× band "the most defensible 'real' figure" for how fast frontier price-for-performance improves, and said that middle range has been reasonably stable. It includes hardware price declines and competition, and removing those leaves the [~3× algorithmic](#c/e-price-algo) floor. It is far below Epoch's [9–900×](#c/e-price-all) all-models headline. It is still a measure of [cost at a fixed capability](#c/fixed-capability), not of what any specific model or bill does, and it rests on benchmarks as proxies for usefulness. It [challenges](#c/c-100x) the ~100×/year summary.

e-price-algo.overview: This is the [price-trend paper](#c/price-paper)'s estimate that **algorithmic efficiency alone** lowers the price of a fixed performance level by about **3× per year**. It was obtained by dividing out hardware price declines and controlling for competition using open models. It is the bottom rung of the chat's hierarchy, "pure algorithmic efficiency, hardware and competition stripped out," and so the most conservative read of genuine technical progress. It lines up closely with Epoch's independent ~3×/year [pre-training efficiency](#c/e-pretrain-eff) estimate. The chat read its smoothness as evidence that [incremental work](#c/c-incremental) dominates. The decomposition depends on modelling choices, and the figure bundles many ingredients (MoE, data, distillation, serving tricks) without separating them. See [Algorithmic efficiency](#c/algorithmic-progress).

e-pretrain-eff.overview: This is [Epoch AI](#c/epoch)'s estimate that **pre-training compute efficiency improves about 3.0× per year**: reaching the same capability takes roughly a third as much training compute each year, thanks to better algorithms, architectures and data. The chat used it to explain why capability decoupled from parameter count. Better methods deliver more capability per parameter and per FLOP, so frontier models could [shrink after GPT-4](#c/e-params-shrink) while benchmark scores kept rising. It closely matches the independent [~3×/year inference-price estimate](#c/e-price-algo) for algorithmic progress. It covers pre-training only, not post-training or inference-time gains. It is an estimate that depends on how "the same capability" is measured. See [Algorithmic efficiency](#c/algorithmic-progress).

e-params-dense.overview: This is [Epoch AI](#c/epoch)'s account of the dense-scaling era: parameter counts grew **1,000×, from 117 million (GPT-1) to 175 billion (GPT-3), in two years**, about **31× per year**. Both sizes were disclosed by OpenAI, which makes this the best-documented stretch of the parameter record. In that era every parameter was used on every token, so size tracked both cost and capability, and bigger models reliably scored higher. The chat set it up as the "simple exponential you'd assume," before the trend [slowed for GPT-4](#c/e-params-gpt4) and then [reversed](#c/e-params-shrink). It shouldn't be extrapolated. The 2022 [Chinchilla](#c/chinchilla) finding and later [MoE](#c/moe) broke the link between parameters and capability. See also GPT-1 and GPT-3.

e-params-gpt4.overview: This is [Epoch AI](#c/epoch)'s account that frontier parameter counts grew about **10× more, from GPT-3's 175B to roughly 1.8 trillion for GPT-4, over two years and nine months**, about **2.3× per year**. That is already much slower than the [31×/year](#c/e-params-dense) of the GPT-1 to GPT-3 period. The 1.8T figure is an **estimate**. OpenAI has not disclosed GPT-4's size, and the chat stressed that closed-model counts rest on leaks and analyst inference. Epoch notes that if the trend had continued, frontier models would now be near 10 trillion parameters. That didn't happen: sizes [shrank after GPT-4](#c/e-params-shrink). It marks the end of the dense-scaling era. See [GPT-4](#c/gpt-4) and [Frontier models keep getting bigger](#c/m-bigger).

e-params-shrink.overview: This is [Epoch AI](#c/epoch)'s finding that in **2023 the trend toward bigger frontier models reversed**. Models that followed GPT-4, such as the original GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet, are probably **about an order of magnitude smaller**: roughly 200B and 400B parameters respectively, against GPT-4's estimated ~1.8T. It was a one-step drop, not a sustained rate. The chat flagged all of these as **estimates**. Anthropic has never published a Claude parameter count, and "3.5 Sonnet ≈ 400B" is an informed analyst guess. The causes it gave were [Chinchilla](#c/chinchilla)-style data scaling and [MoE](#c/moe), which splits total from active parameters. Capability kept rising while size fell, which is part of why [cost at a fixed capability](#c/fixed-capability) could collapse. See [the corrected view](#c/r-smaller).

e-moore.overview: Moore's law is the long-running observation that transistor counts on chips double roughly every **two years**, about **1.41× per year**. It is included here only as a reference point for scale, not as a claim about AI. The chat used it to show how extreme AI's rates are. Epoch's [AI chip compute stock](#c/e-stock) doubles about every 7 months (3.4×/year), and [frontier training compute](#c/e-train) about every 5.2 months (5×/year), several times faster than the classic semiconductor pace. The gap shows that AI compute growth has come mostly from building and buying *more* chips and spending more money, not only from better transistors, which is why [capex](#c/capex) and the [capacity constraint](#c/capacity) matter so much. See [Measured rates](#c/rates).
